utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances today, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Joanna Korner and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, Dragan Krgovic, Aleksandar Aleksic, and Igor Pantelic appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. If there are no housekeeping or related matters, could we have the usher please escort the witness back to the stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Brown. I remind you you're still on your oath. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, if -- I'll give you a moment to get your report out on the various documents. I want to move, fairly swiftly, I hope, through the remainder of your report, Mr. Brown, beginning this morning with the section at page 88 in English, paragraph 2.77, headed "Retaliatory Actions and Killings of Non-Serbs." And effectively, you point out in that paragraph that during and after a number of the attacks, a number of killings and retaliatory actions against non-Serbs were reported in contemporary military and police documents. I'd just like to have a look at a couple of those, please, as examples. Could we look, first of all, please, at document P496, which is at tab 41. And it's referred to in your paragraph 2.80 where you list a number of the killings that came to the attention of the military. And if we look, now, at that document, which is dated the 7th of August of 1992, which is a regular combat report, and we'll see at the bottom of that first page, and I think it's the second page in B/C/S; it is. Second page in B/C/S, at paragraph 3, at the bottom of that paragraph, it says: "About 1,460 POWs were brought from Omarska to Manjaca POW camp. There were deaths during the transport to the camp." I think it's right, Mr. Brown, that you looked at, in fact, after you'd completed this report, a number of documents that emerged after the completion from a captain called Lukajic [phoen], who was at Manjaca. And it was he, the one reporting on a number of these matters.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think he was clearly working at Manjaca camp and most likely, at least from the documents I saw subsequent to writing this report, that he would send reports to the security organ of the corps. And I'm assuming what happened in this report was that that incident was then taken and placed in the daily combat report of the corps and sent to the VRS Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So as far as you can tell from your survey of these documents, was the corps not only reporting matters carried out by members of the corps but also matters that might affect the security, for example, such as this killing outside Manjaca camp?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As I say, you list a number of incidents that appear in the military documents. The Kotor Varos incidents that you deal with at the end of paragraph 2.80, and deals with killings that took place in Kotor Varos, again not by the military. Could we have a look, very quickly, please, at document which is P81.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can we have the tab number?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, sorry. The tab is 20 -- tab 26.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is actually a session of the Kotor Varos Crisis Staff on the 26th of June, which was attended, as we can see from the top, by Lieutenant-Colonel Peulic. And in fact, he -- at the beginning, he presents a report. And at this meeting, a Dr. Gajanin informed the Crisis Staff of the situation as regards casualties and reporting on what had been done on the premises of the health centre by the special unit. And he said that Mr. Djekanovic said he'd told Dubocanin about everything going on. If we now look, please, at the document which is 65 ter 3707, at tab 28. This is a daily -- a regular combat report it's described. 4th of July, so some eight days later. At item 3, we'll see there that the massacre -- it says "... of members of a Special Police detachment in Kotor Varos municipality has additionally aggravated inter-ethnic relations in the area and made the overall security situation more complex." It says "of," but from your examination, Mr. Brown, do you believe this refers to that incident that was described in the original Kotor Varos Crisis Staff document?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, there clearly is either a typo or an ambiguity there, but it would seem, in relation to the timing, that this is more related to the incident from the -- that Colonel Peulic mentioned and that was discussed in the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe it means -- should be "by" rather than "of."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document has not yet been admitted. May it be admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1790, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, the -- moving through, as I say, the report, you point out that there are a number of references to these killings that appear in the report, and so it appears that the corps was on notice. Can we go specifically to one of the major killings, the Mount -- the killing at Mount Vlasic on the 21st of August. And the Court's heard a great deal about it, which you set out in paragraph 2.88. And as you point out, there was -- and, again, we've seen that, a special report from Lieutenant-Colonel Peulic reporting on the incident. And then you reference, at paragraph 2.89, the -- there was a press conference in November of 1992 where General Talic was specifically questioned on the Vlasic Mountain and indeed the Keraterm killings. And perhaps we can just play that, please. That is at -- there is a transcript which you will find. It's P622 -- 622, at divider 54.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "There are at least two incidents of alleged atrocities that have occurred to refugees."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. It's not playing, is it? Your Honours, I'm told there's B/C/S coming through on the English channel for some reason.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: of refugees [indiscernible] in Trnopolje camp to Travnik. Does the military accept any responsibility for these refugees and has the military conducted any investigation of the fate of these refugees, particularly those that were allegedly killed at Keraterm camp and those killed on Vlasic Mountain during a convoy?"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "There are accusations of at least two incidents involving refugees in this area. One involves 100 people -- 50 people in Keraterm, and the other one involves Trnopolje and Mount Vlasic, where people were killed. "Did your men take part in these actions? And the second question was whether any investigations were carried out." "Answer: Well, the army carried out investigation in order to find out if any of our members had by any chance participated in any crimes violating moral principles. We established that the soldiers had not participated, and we criticised the civilian authorities for failing to inform us that the convoy was leaving, as we would have secured it and prevented any disputes about the departure of the convoy."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What struck you about that, Mr. Brown?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think from the documents, at least, General Talic knew who the alleged perpetrators of the Vlasic Mountain were, and that information that he had received had been passed up to the Main Staff in his combat reports. And I think that, at least from his statement there, that he -- he is more interested in whether any soldiers were involved, and yet he clearly knew at that time who had been allegedly involved in the incident and the details of the incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When you say he was more -- he was more interested in -- sorry, more interested in whether any of the soldiers were involved, what would you have expected him to be saying at this stage?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean, he clearly knew what had gone on, and he almost dismisses it in a way by saying, you know, no soldiers were involved and also that, you know, he put some blame on the fact that the convoy -- he wasn't notified of a convoy. So there's a sort of underlying implication he's aware. But, you know, he doesn't -- doesn't really give much away, particularly. Yet he clearly knew that there had been a significant incident. And this wasn't just a small incident; this was a large number of people. It began to draw some significant international attention. And, you know, maybe also echoed some of the comments in his own documents where -- where one of the references is that, you know, it's -- thank goodness the international community hasn't become more aware of it. You know, it's not -- he doesn't seem to show any -- I say sympathy is maybe not the phrase, but anything more than just, you know, the troops weren't involved, and kind of dismisses the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let's have, in fact, a look at a report that contained a reference to this incident a couple of months earlier, shortly afterwards, on the 3rd of September. And it's document, please, P611, at tab 51. Now, this is a report dated the 3rd of September from the 1st Krajina Corps and it's to the Main Staff and also to the psychological and propaganda activities department, state of combat morale in August of 1992. And, in fact, it went out under General Talic's signature. Can we go, please, first of all, to the second page in English, quite on the point that's worth noting this, and the second page in B/C/S. Top of the English page, and it's a little way down in the B/C/S. It's reported that all units and armed formations have essentially been put under the control of the 1st Krajina Corps, although there are still resistance from the CSB. And then if we go to paragraph 2, third page in English, and it's the fourth page in B/C/S. The overall political and security situation in August 1992 was characterised by the following: The activities of several paramilitary governments and armed formations increased extremism towards Muslim and Croatian population, continued efforts to place the organs of the authorities and the MUP above military formations and the army. And then at the bottom of that page: Certain tensions are still presents in the Kotor Varos, Kljuc, Sanski Most, and Prijedor areas because a large number of arrested citizens for whom there is no evidence or criminal reports that they participated in the armed rebellion. Pausing there for a moment. Again, is that a -- were you able to see whether that was a reflection of documents that were coming from the Manjaca camp?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: This last section about individuals not ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There are a number of references in the documents I saw subsequently from Manjaca that that is very evident. And I believe this is not the only document from the documents I was able to review prior to writing this report that the military had reservations that a large number of people of whom were in detention, that there was no evidence whatsoever that they had participated in armed rebellion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then if we carry on. The CSB --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And could we go to the next page in English. Thanks. Still the same page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It says: "The CSB, especially from Prijedor, is not contributing this approach. Prijedor, headed by Stevo Drljaca, who led a convoy of people who wanted to leave the crisis area, they committed a massacre in the Skender Vakuf area of over 150 men who wanted to leave the territory of the Krajina autonomous region. This action caused indignation not only amongst the citizens but also amongst the 1st Krajina Corps soldiers, this dark stain which was created and did not have support. But it is very fortunate that the international community did not find out about it in more detail." Now, I think that's self explanatory. But this report went out under General Talic's name. Would he have had to approve it before it went out or could it -- would it just go out under his name?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I mean, he's the corps commander. And whether a staff officer signs on his behalf, he has the -- it's his authority and it's going to the Main Staff. I don't know if this particular one had his signature; I would have to look at the original B/C/S. But clearly --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The last page in B/C/S, please, I think we'll find it. It looks like somebody signed on his behalf. If we go to the last page in both, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, someone has signed on his behalf. That's not General Talic's signature. But irrespective of that, it's one of his senior staff officers. I would imagine the -- potentially the assistant commander for moral and civilian affairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. You also deal, in paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- 2.92 -- sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I don't know if you were about to leave this document, but I have a question to Mr. Brown. If we go back to, I think it was page 2, where the author of the report states that everything -- all units have now been assembled under the control of the 1st Krajina Corps, except that there is still resistance from the CSB. And I would be curious to know how Mr. Brown had interpreted that comment. Do you know, Mr. Brown?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, the way I read that is it relates to the issue of paramilitary units and potentially the document we discussed last week where paramilitary units were meant to be placed under the control of the -- of the VRS or the corps. In that document, I think there is a reference to the CSB. And maybe this is a reference that, as yet, the CSB hasn't been placed under control. I don't think this reference is all units, all types in the corps; I read this as relating to that discussion or issue of paramilitary units potentially operating outside the authority of the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But how and why would the CSB -- I suppose we are speaking about the CSB in Prijedor. How and why would that CSB offer resistance to the plans of controlling and coordinating all units under the umbrella of the 1st Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think this refers to this -- or potentially refers to -- the way I read it, potentially refers to the special unit, the CSB special units, not the unit from Prijedor particularly. This may relate to this issue around Kotor Varos and the Banja Luka CSB, which was one of the units referred to in that paramilitary document. And also I know that after -- or, I believe, I don't know the full details, but I believe that after the incident in Kotor Varos there was some discussion about resubordinating or placing that CSB under the control of the army, and it may well be that that hadn't been formalised or completed or the discussions hadn't gone particularly well and there was some reservation about placing that CSB under the control of the army. I think I read it as it relating to the CSB special unit Banja Luka, not necessarily the -- well there wasn't a CSB in Prijedor, but SJB or another police organisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I'm not sure I fully understand what it is you're saying. I mean, I suppose that at no point had there been any plans to place the entire CSB or SJB under the control of the army, so the only thing that, as far as I understand it, the only thing we are discussing could be the special unit, which structurally resorted under the -- under the MUP, either the CSB or the SJB or whatever it is in Prijedor, and those special units were placed under the control of the MUP. So my question is now: Are you suggesting that the 1st Krajina Corps attempted to have these special units transferred under its control from the MUP to the army and that the CSB offered resistance to that plan? Is that how you interpret General Talic's remark or, should I say, the remark of the author of the report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think that, from my reading, was possibly what happened. I know that the CSB special unit, Banja Luka special unit, existed. It took part in the operation in Kotor Varos. It obviously conducted some unauthorised activity, which is referenced in the Krajina Corps. And I believe what happened after that was that there were discussions about whether and how the CSB should operate. And it may well have been that one of those discussions, bearing in mind that same unit, is referenced in the paramilitary document from the Main Staff, and that the paramilitary unit document makes reference that paramilitaries should be placed under the control of the army, that the discussions were to place that unit under the control of the army. But clearly, by this reference, that either hadn't happened or the discussions hadn't gone well or it was still ongoing. That's maybe how I read it, although I'm not an expert on the issues of the activities of the MUP and the Banja Luka special unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I guess all of this boils down to the question of whether, to your knowledge, the MUP regarded the special unit as a unit that resorted under its control.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And compared to a unit that was just a paramilitary unit acting more or less independently.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure I can answer that question, sir, because I haven't looked at the relationships within the MUP and looked at their structures and how they operated. I would possibly read from this document that the CSB at this stage isn't -- special unit is not under control of the army, or at least there are problems there in terms of either trying to place it under the control of the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I think this is as far as we can go with this. Thank you, Ms. Korner. Back to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but -- thank you. I think we'd better go back, just briefly, to look at the Main Staff paramilitary document just so we can see what you're referring to. Could we have up again, please, P591, which is tab 36. And we need to go, please, to page 4 in English, and -- let me just find it again in B/C/S. It's -- I think it's the same page, yes, same page. It's not. It's the next page in English, sorry. Page 5 in English -- sorry, it's the fourth page in English, fifth page in B/C/S. Thank you. At the bottom of the fourth page in English, it talks about the SOS under the command of Stevandic, and then it says the officials in the CSB have considerable influence over the SOS, many infamous Banja Luka criminals have joined, part of the SOS formation was officially disbanded, joined the Banja Luka CSB Special Police detachment -- oh, sorry, can we go to the next page in English, please. Joined the Banja Luka CSB Special Police detachment but is not really under the control of the detachment's command or the CSB.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is that what you were referring to, Mr. Brown?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe it's slightly more nuanced here and maybe I would refine a little bit my position, but because clearly there is -- whether it's a component of the CSB and whether this document is referring only to that component or the CSB as a whole, maybe it's unclear. But I do believe that there were discussions in -- in the summer about the CSB and its position and whether it should be commanded by the MUP or whether it should be integrated into the army, I believe. Although, as I say, I'm not an expert on the activities of Banja Luka CSB or the MUP structures.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Then moving swiftly through the last part. You deal in your paragraphs 2.92, effectively till the end of the report, with the killings that took place in Vecici in November of 1992 -- or not Vecici, the -- those who had escaped from Vecici and the killings at the Grabovica school. And I think all we need to do is note that you point out that originally the 1 KK reported this --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, is this incident part of the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic knows it's not on the indictment but nonetheless it's evidence that has been led in this case and has been led before because it goes to the general pattern of the events and also the reporting of the events that it was known to those in authority what had happened. So if there's no further objection, I'll continue my summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we look at your paragraph 2.96, you refer to the 1st Krajina Corps's report that those who had been captured were killed in a massacre. And you reference that report. And it was a report of the 4th of November. And there, as you set out in that paragraph, 40 Green Beret members were killed and 200 were captured. A brutal massacre of the captured members of the Green Berets started because of the wounding of four and the killing of one soldier of the Kotor Varos Light Infantry Brigade, et cetera. And you point -- then go on to point out, in paragraph 2.97, that by the following day the corps was no longer portraying this incident as a massacre but that the deaths were simply combat casualties. And you reference your -- the report of the 1st Krajina Corps the following day, the 5th of November, where they talk about - it's the top of page 97 in English - more than 150 extremists dying in combat and later reporting makes no reference to the incident. It may be clear already but is this one of the themes that you noted, as with the Mount Vlasic massacre, that the reporting was not always strictly accurate or changed?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't say that the reporting wasn't strictly accurate. I think it is. I didn't see this as a pattern particularly that they would change the -- there would be a killing or a reference to a massacre or a slaughter and then that that would be changed. I think this is the only incident that I remember that happening. But there were a number of references, as the report indicates, where the corps was clearly aware that killings had occurred. This was one of more obvious ones, and I don't remember seeing any reference in the documents that anybody was ever held accountable in the -- in the 1st Krajina Corps for this or whether there was any significant investigation into this incident after it happened. And Colonel Peulic, who was the Operations Group Vlasic commander at the time, continued to serve on in the corps for a period of time, and I don't remember seeing anybody held accountable for that, let alone any investigation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Yes, thank you. And the next section of your report deals with the rounding up of the population, the transfer to camps and detention centres. Again, the Court's heard a lot of evidence about this, and you've set this all out in your report. Perhaps just a couple of things that we ought to note. You talk about the -- in paragraph 2.103, page 99 in English, the conclusions of the Sanski Most Crisis Staff - I'm not going to turn up the document because we've seen it - putting the prisoners into categories. And you point out that -- it ends by saying: In view of this, have a talk with Colonel Stevilovic from the 1st Krajina Corps. Are you able to assist the Court: Why would that have involved a conversation with Colonel Stevilovic?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Stevilovic was the security -- senior security officer in the corps, and I assume that the issue of captured individuals would have had a security implication with him. And whether they wanted to have some commonality across the corps or whether they wanted just to inform him that individuals that may be coming in to Manjaca camp, for example, would be classified in this manner. So I guess it's because it has a security implication that's been referenced that they want to discuss that with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And then you point out in the next paragraph that the classification drawn up for those who were sent to Omarska was pretty similar. You deal with, as I say, I want to go through this fairly quickly, the paragraph 2.110, although the police were primarily responsibility for the running of the camp, the military were also involved in the processing of prisoners in Omarska. And you've set all that out. And, as I say, the Court has heard a great deal of evidence about this. Can we, however, go to the corps's awareness, not only of what was happening in Manjaca camp but in other camps as well. You reference that in paragraph 2.122, which we've looked at already, that the corps was aware that killings had returned -- that killings had occurred during the transfer of prisoners from Omarska. And then can we look at what they knew about Keraterm, paragraph 2.125? In July -- 25th of July -- sorry, it's the paragraph before 2.124. On 25th of July 1992, a daily corps report informed the Main Staff that prisoners attempted to escape, mass escape, and 50 prisoners were killed. And then there was a general report, and I think we ought to look at that, please. That's document 2874, 65 ter 2874, at tab 50. This is dated the 22nd of August, and it's sent to the Prijedor operative group command, to the command in person. Do you know who was the commander of the Prijedor operative group?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe at that time it was Lieutenant-Colonel Arsic who was also commander of the 343rd or the 43rd motorised brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And it sets out the situation in Prijedor can be summed up in the following sentence: Nevertheless discipline, nevermore waywardness. Can we go to the second page in English, please. And the second page, I think, in B/C/S. At the top of the page, it says, another interesting item: All are now washing their hands regarding the camps and reception centres, attempting to pass responsibility for issuing orders for mass execution of civilians in the camps and centres on to someone else. This has become particularly noticeable since the visit of foreign reporters to Prijedor, more precisely, to Omarska and Trnopolje. This report is August the 22nd. Is it clear who the report is from?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not. Not from the reading -- my reading, it's not clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. But it apparently comes from the command of the Doboj operative group; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think -- I think -- well, I think the information has -- the forward command post of the corps at this time was towards the corridor area, and I think what's happened is information has come to the forward command post and they've relayed that information in entirety to Prijedor operative group command and maybe they've just used the stamp from Operative Group Doboj because that's quite close to where the forward command post was. But it's not clear where the information originated from.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And you say -- in fact, I think you say in your report that you looked at other reports from the same day, in fact, one about deserters, which is referenced in your -- which was, in fact, signed by General Talic and -- but comes with a similar stamp.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe General Talic was probably at the forward command post at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then it goes on to say: "One thing is certain: We are already starting to feel the cost of the needless spilling of Muslim blood. There is information that Muslims driven out of the municipality of Prijedor and those who have fled to the other side but who had done nothing against the Serbian Republic before are now taking up arms in Croatia and joining the war against us. "In addition to this, Muslims who were either driven out of or fled from Prijedor to Croatia now attack everything that is Serbian, and the Serbs in Croatia have thus gained fanatical enemies, bequeathed to them by the civilian and military authorities of Prijedor." How does this report, Mr. Brown, fit in with the army's view of what was happening?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure I can say, well, the army's view of what was happening, but it's clear that the army have been made aware that -- about the situation in Prijedor. That a large number of people have been driven out, that their detention camps have become known in the international community. And the military clearly, or the author, is clearly aware that this has now caused significant problems, not just because of the incidents on their own, but because by driving people out, those who had been driven out are now potentially signing up to fight the republic, Serb Republic. So sort of on all levels the activities of what's gone on in Prijedor with the civilian and military authorities operations there has caused significant problems. And it's not the only document I've seen that they were aware, I mean, we talked about killings and other things, but this would seem to crystallise what had happened, that it's come out in the international community after the visits of camps. And what they're not doing is denying any of this driving Muslims out, the issue of camps; they're not denying that this has not gone on. What they're saying is it's caused significant problems and that it's going to continue to cause us a military problem because individuals who have been driven out will be coming back to, in essence, to conduct operations against us or to fight against us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could that be admitted and marked, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P1791, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, just --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, did His Honour Judge Delvoie want to say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner. Mr. Brown, at the end of the first paragraph of the document that was just on the screen, it is said, if I remember correctly, the impression is that the local fatherland front is behind all of this. Something to that effect. I don't have it on the screen any more, so I can't --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we have it back again, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It's on page 2. The impression is that the local fatherland front is involved in all this. What is this about? What is the local fatherland front; do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm unaware what that is, sir. I -- that is the only time I've seen that reference, and I'm not clear what it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That's why I asked. Because it's the first time I see it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think that's the same for all of us, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then can we just, as I say, go back to your report and very quickly note, as you have dealt with already, that in paragraph 2.127, the fact that the corps was aware that people were being imprisoned against whom there was no evidence. And finally, at 2.131, you point out that the military were also involved in the final removal of many of the prisoners who had found themselves in detention camps in the Bosanska Krajina area and make the point that the transport wasn't back to their own homes but out of the Serbian Republic. If we look, please, at just one example of that. It's the document at -- it's 65 ter 1569, at paragraph -- at tab 60. This is dated the 15th of December, and it's an order from General Talic to close down Manjaca. Prisoners for whom investigation has -- so far has not determined they're committing war crimes shall be handed over to the International Red Cross. And then prisoners for whom there are grounds for suspicion they have committed criminal acts or crimes against humanity or war crimes shall be sent to Batkovici, in paragraph 3. Some, however, of the prisoners from the first group shall be sent to Kula in order to be exchanged for Serbian prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And Your Honours, can that be admitted and marked, please. That's not yet an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P1792, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And can I deal with one other document. I'm sorry it's completely out of context, but I omitted to deal with it. And because it's right next door to the one we just dealt with. Can we have a look, please, at 65 ter 3706, at tab 59, which really came in, in one of the earlier sections you were talking about last week.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is an order dated the 26th of November by General Talic, ordering the -- it's called resubordination of some artillery pieces because they're required by the Banja Luka CSB police brigade. And I think we looked at the documents for that last week.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's related to that period where a large police brigade is formed and for operations in the corridor, and I guess they are giving them some artillery.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I should have dealt with that last week, but I forgot. Could I have that admitted and marked as well, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P1793, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Returning, then, to your report and briefly on the detention centres and camps, I think you note, finally, in the last paragraph on this section 2.133, that, effectively, this was an overlapping - and this is the middle of the paragraph - involvement of military police and civilian authorities in relation to the establishment and running of many of these facilities, and the fact that a significant number of detainees were transferred between multiple camps highlights a degree of planning and cooperation. Turning, then, next, please, to the removal of the non-Serb population from towns and villages, which is at -- begins at paragraph 2.134. Again, the Court's heard a lot of evidence about this, so I'm not proposing to really take you through the paragraphs of that report. You've already dealt with the fact that the corps was clearly aware of the expulsion of the non-Serb population, and there are a number of references in its reports. And if we look, please, at just one of these documents. Could we have a look, please, at P432.17, at tab 23. Again, this is a report, this time the 14th of June, on the state of combat morale. And if we go, please, to the second page in English and the second page in B/C/S, paragraph 2, the effects of the political security situation on the territory on combat morale. It talks about the complex political and security situation in BH in May escalating into numerous armed conflicts in a large number of towns in Bosnian Krajina, and references Kljuc, Sanski Most, Prijedor, and Jajce, and asserts that all these conflicts were organised by the BH, TO, and in conjunction with the Republic of Croatia, and were imposed upon the Serbian People. And, again, you've dealt with that aspect in some of the incidents you say which then led to these reprisals. Second part of that document, that paragraph: In our estimate, a certain degree of chaos and total inter-ethnic war have been forestalled. This is confirmed by the continuously stable conditions in Banja Luka and many other towns, as well as by the way in which control has been established in Kotor Varos, where a real explosion of armed conflicts was threatening to erupt. And then, please, the third page in English, and the fourth page in B/C/S. At the end of that paragraph, sorry, the section just before we get to paragraph 3, the report asserts: The most difficult situation concerns the Muslim and Croat refugees in the area of AR Krajina, their security and the provision of food. The attempt to expel them to Central Bosnia failed because of transportation difficulties and their resistance to leaving their places of residence. This is giving rise to vindictiveness and revenge and is resulting in the enemy closing its ranks. You note in your report at paragraph 2.148 that the military were not overtly critical of this policy or appeared to hold any genuine sympathy for the plight of the non-Serbs. If anything they were critical that the policy of expulsion was not working, simply due to logistic problems and resistance from the non-Serbs who didn't want to leave their home. Was that view one that you formed simply as a result of this document, the lack of sympathy, or from your overall review of these documents?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think it is -- it is true that -- in this particular reference, that they -- they are aware, firstly, that people are being expelled, non-Serbs are being expelled, but they are not giving any -- they don't seem to have any sympathy particularly, they were just saying that the logistic problems were causing that. They were also referencing the fact that -- the fact that there are -- they haven't been expelled is giving rise to vindictiveness, presumably meaning robbery or looting or attacks on non-Serbs, but they're not -- they're almost implying that if they had been expelled then that wouldn't have happened. And also, again, this issue that is -- this revenge issue and the enemy closing its ranks. So there doesn't seem to be any -- well, there's certainly no reference that this type of activity should stop, that it's unacceptable, that we are -- we should be -- we are fighting or taking control of territory for -- irrespective of ethnicity. And it's not just this incident. There are other references. And I think the general tenor of the corps reports in this would give very little sympathy whatsoever for -- for the -- for the non-Serbs. You know, if we look at the references in the documents where people are in detention centres and the military are making references themselves that individuals have -- there's no evidence that any of these -- or many of these individuals were involved in activities. The follow-on would usually or you would expect it to be that, well, these people should be released, or we should make measures for those people to be taken back to their places of residence in -- but there's none of that. So from the -- many of the military documents I don't see any sympathetic -- particularly sympathetic language. Maybe this is a clear example of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. And you then -- yes, you deal with the -- in your further paragraphs - and as I say, I'm not going to deal with them in any detail at all - the fact that the military was apparently getting reports of how many people had actually been moved out. Coming, then, to destruction and looting, which is at page 122 of your report. You state, in paragraph 2.164, that the municipality operations in Bosanska Krajina not only marked by the large-scale movement of population but noted for significant levels of destruction during and after military attacks and high level of looting. And you point out, if we move to 2.177, that it was a -- the issue was a complex one, face value, the corps appears to take action to stop it, for example, as you pointed out earlier, by issuing instructions to stop blowing up religious institutions. But there was a clear distinction between the cases of individual, small-group looting which the war profiteering speculation which the 1st Krajina Corps were critical of and the attempted to curtail and an officially sanctioned policy which enabled the Bosnian Serb authorities to appropriate property, et cetera. And I don't think that we need to go into any of the documents. At page 131 of your report, paragraph 2.189, you deal with the commendations that were handed out, as you've already mentioned. On the 11th of May, General Talic congratulated the soldiers and command of the 6th Brigade for liberating Krupa after the attacks of Hambarine and Kozarac. The 43rd Motorised Brigade was congratulated. And you've already mentioned the various awards handed out to paramilitaries. And then finally, your -- on this aspect, at page 133, you deal with the non-Serb armed resistance. And that's summarised, effectively, at paragraph 2.209. Where you say it's evident that a defensive structure was being established in some non-Serb areas, certain limited weaponry was available, and you then make the comparison between the non-Serbs and the VRS. And I think, Mr. Brown, we really dealt with it earlier when you say that the VRS, if one looks at the numbers it contained and the armaments, was considerably superior; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. It would seem so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And can I turn finally, before we get -- look at the Mladic notebooks, to the question of the operations in the corridor. Because that's a -- quite an important part of your report. At page 140, you deal with the operations in the corridor and Jajce. We looked at, last week, the strategic goals that were issued at the 12th of May Assembly, and you point out in paragraph 2.213 that General Talic himself in an interview, which I'm not going to trouble you with, set out the aims of the operation. We'll see some references to it but can we have a look, please, in the Mladic notebooks, first of all, at the directive from the Main Staff which when you wrote the report you had not seen but you have now seen. Can we look, please, at document 2624, at tab 19. Now, this is a directive -- I think if we look at the last page, please, in each document, which goes out under the name of the commander, Main Staff, Mladic. And it's addressed to the 1st and 2nd Krajina Corps, the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, and Eastern Bosnia. If we go, please, then, back to the second page, well, it's still the first page in English -- first page in -- sorry, second page in English, first page in B/C/S. We see the goal of the action. First of all, secure parts of Sarajevo in A. So this is going wider, is it, than just the corridor operation?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is actually for the -- for all the corps of the VRS at this stage, but in particular I think it's stressing activities in Sarajevo, which was to secure the Serbian part of Sarajevo, which actually was also a strategic goal. And also the issue of the corridor. And that involved the 1st Krajina Corps and also the East Bosnia Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now let's just look at the corridor. It says: B, ensure -- I think we need to go to the second page in B/C/S. Ensure contact between Semberija and the Bosnian Krajina. And then, third page in English, same page in B/C/S. First of all, it talks about, again, Sarajevo at the top of that page, and it says: Group forces to open the corridor between Semberija and the Bosnian Krajina. And in the second stage, in a duration of four to six days, create the corridor between Semberija and the Bosnian Krajina, reject enemy forces away from the communications. In the period to come, extend the corridor permanently, providing secure traffic communication in it. So there was to be approximately, what, eight days to create the corridor altogether?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to secure the -- that route initially, and then it was meant to be expanded, I think, later.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may that be marked and admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1794, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And now can we look, please, at the 9th of June order that was issued by General Talic following on from that directive, which is document 10641, at tab 20.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It says: Order by the 1st Krajina Corps command. Enclosed we submit the order for the Defence security and active operations of the command of the 1st Krajina Corps. And it's actually -- it appears to be signed. It says: Standing in for chief of operations, Colonel Krajnc. Do you know who Colonel Krajnc was?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was a JNA or former JNA officer, I believe, a Croat. And he -- he was in the operations department of the corps, but he was removed, I believe, not long after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And then if we go on to -- it gives the distribution list, done in 21 copies and distributed to ... and you can see if we go ... and then can we go, please, to page -- the fourth page in English and also the fourth page in B/C/S. It's the order, the Defence security and territory and offensive operations, and it begins with 1, the enemy -- enemy forces are deployed throughout the territory and zone of responsibility of the 1st Krajina Corps. And it goes on to say: In areas where armed conflicts have not yet occurred, arming of Muslim and Croatian population has already been carried out, and they can spring into action at the required moment. All capable of bearing arms are military personnel. And they will not refrain from using all available weapons. Do. You have any comment on that, Mr. Brown?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it sets quite a tone for the corps. I mean, this is being passed down to all the subordinate formations in the corps. And General Talic is indicating that at least he views that anybody who can carry weapons is a -- should be treated as military personnel. And I'm assuming he's meaning the non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then, organised actions by Muslim formations can be expected very soon in the areas of Gradiska, Kotor Varos. We know, Mr. Brown, that the takeover of Kotor Varos took place in fact two days after this. Is there any connection between that and this beginning of operations that you were able to see?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because he's -- he does give tasks not only to the units that are going to be involved in the operation in the corridor but he is making tasks for all the other units in -- in the other areas to secure the territory or to continue to secure the territory, to take measures to secure the territory. And I'd have to quickly look at it, but it --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, we're going to go through it. Can we go to page -- as you say, he's setting out tasks of the 1st Krajina -- the next page, tasks of the 1st Krajina Corps, then the neighbouring forces. And then if we look at page 6 in English, and I believe it's page 3 in -- sorry, page 4 in B/C/S as well. Not page 4. I'm so sorry. It's page -- it says page 4 at the top, but it's probably the sixth - one, two, three, four - sixth page in B/C/S. And it's the sixth page in English. At the top of the -- 4: I have decided to continue with persistent and active defences increasing measures against possible surprise actions or creation of new flash points, speed up the clearing of the territory and the elimination of any -- any -- of any enemy hotbeds in the zone of responsibility. And then the first -- the offensive parts of the operation planned out and carried out in three stages. And it talks, summarising. It's a very long order. It effectively is the Operation Corridor, talks about widening the corridor. And then the second stage of the operation beginning on the 11th of June.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And going back to your previous question, just having quickly looked at the document. On page 8 --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, coming to that.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- it references the 122nd Brigade which was the brigade along with the Kotor Varos light brigade that was dealing with Kotor Varos. And Talic instructs it to continue active operations in that area, closing routes from basically Central Bosnia into Kotor Varos, continue eliminating trouble spots, prevent the emergence of new sources of conflict, step up measures of full control over the territory, prevent infiltration. And I think that that instruction was passed on to the 122nd Brigade and that that -- what followed from that were operations in vote Kotor Varos which occurred not long after this instruction was issued.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see the time. I've got two other matters to deal with on this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we take the break and resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just for the record, Your Honours, Stanisic Defence has been joined by Ms. Suzanna Mohr and Ms. Alexandra Laskowski. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. So noted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, just a couple of further matters on this document. Can we go, please, to page 11 in English and page 9 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, Ms. Korner, can you tell me what tab it is again?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, I'm so sorry. It's tab 20. Where there's a section dealing with operations support where it states, in the second paragraph, under A: Monitor the activity of the Muslim and Croat population in areas where there are no conflicts and detect, in time, the beginning, the objectives, and the modes of involvement of these formations. And under --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm terribly sorry. We are not getting this in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is it not on page 9 -- oh, no, you're on page 6. Sorry, 9 at the top of --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So it must be three pages further on. Yeah. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then under B, security support, we see that it's terminating sabotage, terrorists, and spying activities by the enemy's Special Forces, especially on the axes that lead from Cazin Krajina, Lasva valley into the zone of the corps, and in areas with Muslims and Croatian population where there have been no conflicts. And then finally this: Devote -- sorry, you need to go to the next page in B/C/S, please. Yes, thank you. Devote special attention to security for protection of sensitive elements of combat disposition, achieve full control and restrict movements of the population in the zone of responsibility. After they are processed by intelligence and security organs of the units, take prisoners of war and persons responsible for hostile activity with the required paper work to camps for prisoners of war. Was this a particularly wide-ranging order, Mr. Brown, in terms of everything that was set out, or were there other similar orders that you saw?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This was a particularly wide-ranging order. But I believe, also, after the other directives were passed, for example, Operational Directive 3, which I think was in August, I believe General Talic passed a similar -- you know, did the similar process of passing an instruction down to his corps. But this is quite a wide-ranging order to his subordinate formations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm terribly sorry to -- but I see in the English translation that the last word "viz," v-i-z, it says "expansion unknown." I believe it refers to the military investigative prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You may well -- Mr. Zecevic ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, do you know what it refers to?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do believe that's what it refers to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Zecevic. Yes, that's all I want to ask about that document. Your Honours, may that be admitted, please and marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P1795, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, a -- I think you also looked at, recovered from the 1st Krajina Corps headquarters, a map of the operation. Can we go -- could we have up, please -- it's at tab 63, and it's document number 3710. And there is a translation. Tab 63. I think we need to have the translation up as well, please, at the same time. Try and have it at the same time, anyhow. I think we can see it says, at the left-hand side, I approve, Lieutenant General Ratko Mladic; then a decision, 1st Krajina Corps commander to carry out offensive operations; and then, military secret, strictly confidential, corridor 92. And then we can -- there's a key to this. Did it appear that there was any involvement by any kind of police brigades in this?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to see the -- if you're asking me whether it's highlighted on this map --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I would have to see the map itself. It's a very large -- from what I remember, it's been a long time now, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I think it's a very large map, but I do know that there were police -- there was police involvement. I know specifically that there was police involvement from the RSK MUP and it took part in that operation, and, in fact, I think after the success of the operation, there was a hesitancy or an instruction that that police formation was not to be publicly congratulated, that it would be congratulated in a different way. But I know that there was an RSK MUP involvement, and I'd have to check to see whether there was Krajina MUP involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Yes, I think if you look at your paragraph 2.217, where you state the importance of the corridor operation and the overall activity of the 1st Krajina Corps cannot be overstated, scale of the operation, the high degree of planning, coordination required. 1st Krajina Corps, East Bosna Corps, and forces from the RSK MUP were involved. And the relatively quick success of the operation were testimonies to the abilities of the VRS and the 1st Krajina Corps. And, as you say, most importantly, however, with the creation of the corridor link from the Krajina, one of the strategic goals was achieved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, I think I have put the question that I'm going to put to you now already, but I'm going to bring it up again in order for you to expand a bit on the active role that the RSK MUP took in this operation. Do you know if the MUP officers took part in the tactical combat, as combatants, or did they participate in securing the civilian tasks that would follow from the completion of the military tactical operation? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would -- I have to say I've not looked at the role of the RSK MUP in that operation and the detail of what they had done. I would -- I would have to go back through the documents before I would make a more accurate judgement of that. My feeling is that they were involved as a formed unit to conduct operations there, but the detail of what that may have meant in terms of whether they were securing an area, processing prisoners, mounting check-points, or whether they were operating as a normal infantry unit, for example, might have operated, I am unclear, but they were a significant component. And I think there are a number of documents showing gratitude by the VRS Main Staff for their involvement. And, in a way, it doesn't surprise me that they were involved because one of the -- there were a number of reasons why the corridor was important, and I make no bones that the corridor was severed and that put the Krajina in a difficult position because it was severed from other parts, but when Karadzic announced the importance of the corridor, he didn't just say it was because the Krajina is isolated. He indicated, -- and he put it as the second most important strategic goal, he indicated that to achieve success in the corridor allowed all the Serb areas in Bosnia to be united but it also allowed the Serb areas in Bosnia to be united with the Serb areas in Croatia, and those two areas to be united with Serbia. So in essence, it unified all the areas, and so for that -- for that reason it doesn't surprise me that the RSK MUP were there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. We are perfectly aware of the importance and the significance of this operation. My question was more about the actual nature of the tasks that the RSK MUP were able to offer during this operation. And as you say, the -- either they could have taken part as an infantry unit directly involved in the combat as such, or they could have assisted in providing the civilian functions that would normally follow from any tactical operation. But I think you have made your point clear. Thank you very much. Back to you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we look at the -- your paragraph 2.215, you refer there to Martic's MUP forces, the RSK, attacking in two areas, the reference for that being a Banja Luka documentary Operation Corridor. Does that help you at all, or not?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I would like to read the transcript again to refresh my memory on what the video says. And whether it's just a one-liner or whether it's more expansive, I don't know, but I guess I would have to review the document to be -- maybe to answer His Honour's question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, it -- unfortunately, it wasn't one of our -- it wasn't on our 65 ter list. And at that stage I didn't realise that it was a matter of interest. But we can actually get ahold of the transcript of that video and give it to the witness, if there's no objection, so he could look at it in the next break. We'll make arrangements to do that. Without, obviously, any comment from us or questions. Now, Your Honours, sorry, could I ask that this map be admitted and marked, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P1796, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you note in the same paragraph that deals with Martic's MUP forces that there were two stages of the operation, firstly towards Modrica, which they captured by the 29th of June; and then the second, axis towards Derventa by the 4th of July. And so you point out that a corridor link was actually achieved with the seize of Modrica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So if the operation started -- well, the order is dated the 9th of June, and it says the second stage shall be the 11th of June. So roughly two weeks or so to get through the first stage; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Seems only a matter of weeks that they achieved their goal.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you've already pointed out that it was one of the most important operations, certainly in 1992. I don't want to deal with Operation Vrbas in any detail. The last sections of -- oh, well, perhaps I should look at one more, sorry, one more document on this. Can we look at directive 2 which is document number 2644, at tab 33.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, while that's being brought up, I'm told that, contrary to what I thought, it is actually already -- the video is already an exhibit, the liberation of the corridor, and it's P1293. I still think probably the easiest way to deal with this is for Mr. Brown to have a look at it in the break. This is directive number 2, dated the 22nd of July. And, again, it's fairly lengthy. If we look at the last page, it goes out under Mladic's authority, although it's apparently compiled by Major-General Milovanovic. And if we go back please to the first page in both B/C/S and English, this is dealing with the cease-fire agreement. And it says, in the beginning, the first paragraph: The initiator, which was the Serbian Republic Presidency, the significant triumphs of our army which, in fact, encircles the whole territory of the Serbian Republic, the Serbian People, and the army have achieved significant military and diplomatic victories at home and abroad. And then directive, under item 1, I suppose 1.1: We liberated the territory we considered ours, created conditions for political and military leadership. And then 4: We have broken through the corridors in Eastern Bosnia and the Bosanska Posavina and thus made possible the centuries' long aspiration of the Serbian People from BiH and the Serbian Republic of Krajina to be joined with the fatherland, Serbia. So, here, the Serbian Republic of Krajina is, as you stated it, is the RSK, is it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's what he's referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah. And so he's noting, so that there'll be no doubt about it, is that right, the fact that this was a success -- the corridor operation was a successful one?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, may that be admitted and marked, then, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P1797, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The remainder of your report, Mr. Brown, I'm not going to highlight anything in particular, simply because of lack of time, but you dealt with the information and communications issues, and the key themes, paragraph 2.228 following it, you dealt with, in the next chapter, at page 157 - and, as I say, I don't think you need turn it up - cooperation with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. I don't think there's any doubt, is there, and I don't think there's any argument that throughout this period of 1992 there was significant cooperation between Serbia and the Bosnian Serb Republic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was cooperation in particular with the army, the requirement to have weapons, ammunition, funding.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And then you deal thereafter with the roles, responsibility, and authority of the commander, which includes a section on the disciplinary issues, and we've dealt in brief with the disciplinary side of that, as it affected resubordination. And finally the laws and regulations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I make it clear that although I'm not taking Mr. Brown through it, simply through lack of time, we do rely on those sections as well. Mr. Brown, can I now turn, please, to your examination of the Mladic notebooks, which clearly you had not seen at the time that you wrote this report because nobody had them at that stage. Now, I think you point out in the expert report - Your Honour, which we are going to ask to be admitted as well - that you made after you'd looked at the -- sorry -- the various amounts of material which came -- yes, it's the review of the Mladic diaries. And you set out there clearly the documentation that you looked at, which was not just the diaries but other matters, and those sections which you considered were material and relevant to your -- some of the themes in your report. Can I just ask you this, please: Can you -- first of all, can you explain what exactly are these notebooks? I mean, obviously they are compiled by Mladic, but why would a military officer be keeping these sort of notebooks?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the JNA officers or senior JNA officers were required to keep a notebook. I've seen similar types of notebooks before. And they are, as they seem to be, bullet points, references, comments, on the activities of General Mladic. And I'd seen similar kind of diaries before.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And I want to look, please, if I may, to some of the references that -- not all of them but some, indeed. Can we go, please, to, I think, the 6th of May is the first entry that I want to discuss with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I also ask that -- as you'll see, they were all MFI'd at the time, until Mr. Hannis decided which ones should be asked to be admitted exhibits; he put in a note to the Trial Chamber, and I wonder if the MFI could be lifted now before we go any further?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, we have seen the report by Mr. Hannis, and it occurs to us that we may have to look at it a little more before we simply lift the MFI status.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Very well, Your Honour. At the end of today, anyhow, there's a matter I want to raise -- sorry. At the end of today, there's a matter I want to raise in respect of the notebooks, in any event. But I'll wait until then.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I said the 6th of May. Can we just start, just briefly, on the 21st of February of 1992, and can we go, please -- this is -- it's P1753, and can we go to page 42 in English and 44 in B/C/S. I suppose, putting it in context, this is a -- the heading of the 21st of February is "Tasks." And if we look at page 42, people for the Krajina MUP give blue clothing to the MUP, they are asking for tanks, armoured personnel, helicopters. They can only get armoured combat vehicles which should be repainted, a map of Krajina, map of the Krajina MUP. Mladic is dealing there with what, the MUP in BiH or the MUP in the RSK?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it's the RSK. He was the Knin commander, corps commander, then. There are one or two references, I believe, to the JNA providing men. I think this extract at the top says provide three people for the Krajina MUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA is to provide that. And then I think there are a number of -- one or two other references about the provision of weapons by the JNA to the MUP there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Well, that's what I wanted to -- the next part I want to look at, then. Could we look at page 43 in English and 45 in B/C/S. It says: First stock TO weapons, do that publicly according to the two-key system. And the second part: Secretly. Do you know what the two-key system was?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was a process by which weapons would be -- and I forget if it was part of one of the agreements in the early part of 1992, one of the agreements to end the conflict in Croatia whereby weapons were to be stored in TO armouries and there was to be a two-key process that if these weapons were required they needed the -- then they could be accessed. I don't know the full details, and maybe it relates to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, again, this is, again, the RSK, the Croatian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This is in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we now move then, please, as I said, to the 6th of May. And that's at page 250 -- P1753 still, 258 in English and 265 in B/C/S. Actually, I'm sorry, can we go back to 25 -- I'm so sorry, I missed one out, 255 first of all, in English. I'm sorry. It's the first entry for the 6th of May. And so it will be, sorry, page 55 in English. Sorry. Sorry. 255 is the page number in the diary, I'm so sorry. It's three pages before 58. It should be page 55 in English -- oh, no, sorry, 2 -- it's 253 in English, sorry. Yes, my fault. And 255 in -- no. That's not right. All right. It wasn't on my list. It should, however, say 2 -- page 255 at the top part which is the diary page and 253 at the bottom. Okay. All right. 317, please, then. That's it. Thank you. And what's it in B/C/S? 259 in B/C/S. Yes, thank you. Brilliant.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is the 6th of May, and somebody called General Mandaric is reporting. First of all, who was General Mandaric; do you know?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure, Ms. Korner. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. All right. But he goes on, and this is Mladic recording it, that in Bratunac representatives of the SDS are killing all Muslims by slitting their throats. Two detachments of the Bratunac TO and so on and so forth. And, again, does that show that the army was getting reports of what was happening in these places?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And this was very much at the period when the JNA was -- or the status of the JNA in Bosnia had -- was being agreed. And I believe also on this day General Mladic met with the senior SDS figures.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, we're coming on to that now.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we look now at what should be page 25 -- 256 in the hopes that's right. No. No. 258. Okay. 258 in English. Yes. Is that -- then we saw talks, at 1920 hours on the 6th of May, with Karadzic, Krajisnik, Adzic, and a group of generals from BH.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And we see there, problems, Chief of Staff, et cetera, insignia uniforms; what are they discussing there?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe this meeting to be one of the first, maybe the first, meetings on the establishment of the VRS. And the senior generals from BH are meeting with the senior SDS leadership to discuss the organisation of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we can go, please, to the next page in B/C/S and English, at least I hope it is. Yeah. Yes. And that shows: We control all corridors except one. We will soon be one state and one army. And at the bottom: Later we will unite with the FRY but we will not annex anything to Serbia. And all of this is being said by Karadzic, is that right, as we saw on the previous page?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would seem to be that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And then moving to the next page, 261, we are on the threshold of achieving our centuries' old dream of creating our own state without many internal enemies. Is that a theme that we saw repeated, in fact, in the actual assembly six days later?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and, in fact, I think a similar phrase is used at the Assembly session. And there are other references I noted, I believe, a small number of references to that type of language in the military documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then, finally, on this entry, at 262: We are thinking about forming our armed forces and TO, we rejected any kind of joint army, there will be no joint Bosnian army, the Israeli Defence system is excellent and to crush the green. And in English certainly it's put in "/the Muslims". All right. Can we now move to the following day, the 7th of May. And that is at page 264. Sorry, I beg your pardon. Can we start at 263, please, first of all. Sorry. We see General Adzic, who was who at that stage?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Adzic was the, in essence, commander of the JNA as it was, but the senior officer in the FRY, military officer, presumably come over from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And then he talks about the BH army being named as soon as possible and then various other matters raised. Until we come down to quick mobilisation. Did that happen, a quick mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, within a few weeks there was the mobilisation instruction passed -- being passed out in relation to the VRS, and a flurry of documents relate to that in the forthcoming weeks after this meeting. And, of course, it was referenced as being of importance at the 16th Assembly session.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Then next day, 7th of May, if we just can go up the page a bit. Then there were talks with the vice-president of the FRY, Branko Kostic, and Major General Krstic is apparently there as well. And then if we go to the next page, at 267, thank you. This is another meeting, at 1600 hours, and apparently it's Krajisnik, and I think we can see there he -- the six strategic goals have been set out; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can we go over the page, please. Actually, let's go to 269, skip a page. I don't want to ask you about this one. Now, can you tell us, Mr. Brown, what this appears to be?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would assess that this, bearing in mind the decisions and the discussions beforehand in the meetings we've just looked at, that this is, if you like, a provisional outline of what the VRS is to consist of in relation to the corps and units, and in essence transforming the already-existing or remaining components of the JNA corps into the VRS. So some of the units -- where it says 1st Krajina Corps, 2nd Krajina Corps, that's where they assess the army should be located and that it should consist of these corps and that some of these formations, underneath, for example, where it says East Bosna Corps Bijeljina, and says 17th underneath that, was formerly the JNA 17th Corps. 5th underneath 1st Krajina Corps; that was formerly the JNA 5th Corps. So I think it's an initial sketch, if you like, or layout of what the VRS was to consist of.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. It includes at the bottom a little box that says, "town command." Now, how many documents or what -- how often does this particular aspect of the structure seem to appear?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not seen the phrase "town command" used regularly. In fact, I think this and possibly one other reference in a municipality Crisis Staff document in Kljuc is the only reference I've had to town commands, but I assume that or would assess that what's being sketched out here relates to the former structure of the district TO. I think I mentioned that a little bit a couple of days ago, that in the TO structure, there were district TO commands, and the TO was separate to the JNA, and there was -- which was based on republican level command. So there was a republic-level TO, there was a district-level TO, and beneath that were TOs linked to municipalities. And there were National Defence at municipalities.
