And I look at that maybe in relation to Mladic saying, "We need to absorb or take control or integrate the former TO structure into the new VRS." But in relation to the phrase "town command," I think this and one other is the only reference. There may have been some references, I think, possibly - it's not something I've looked at in great detail for sometime - but the All People's Defence may have references to town commands. But in relation to the documents, I haven't seen that used.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Yes, thank you. That's all I want to ask about that entry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go now, please, to the 2nd of June entry, P1755, page 52, please, to start with. Page 52. The next page. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is a meeting in Banja Luka on the 2nd of June with the leaderships of Banja Luka, Bosnian Krajina, the SRK, and the unit commanders of the 1st Krajina Corps. And Karadzic is speaking. And can we go to the next page, which is 53. He talks about that they ought not to proclaim linking up because it would give Tudjman a pretext to throw out the UN. And then Radislav Brdjanin speaks, and he says, at the bottom of that page, "We have said we are in favour of everything being under the command of the army and for the dissolution of all paramilitary organisations." Can we go to the next page, please, in English. And then General Mladic to agree tacitly, with either M or with Torb, the enemy be kept as busy as possible. The problem of the Krajina, 14,500 Muslims. And then finally on that, can we go to the next page in English, 55. And it will also be 55, I think, in B/C/S. One uniform, one insignia, about prisoners and refugees, a position, please, at the highest level. Were these discussions with -- between the military and the political figures, if you like, the civilian, a feature of these work books?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they appear to be. There were a lot of references of Mladic meeting, actually down to quite a lowish level, down at municipality or in this case at the regional level, and they do seem -- he does seem to have got about, if that's a phrase, and here we have one in Banja Luka, and they are obviously discussing significant issues. The corridor crops up at this meeting. I assume that the Martic reference is Milan Martic from the RSK, so they're discussing the unity between the RSK and Bosnia. And there's differences about whether unifying publicly would be a good thing or not. I think in this meeting there's also a reference by Mr. Brdjanin about Crisis Staffs, everything's being done at Crisis Staff level because that's how it works. Here there is a clearly a question about prisoners and refugees, and they want to know what they should do with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Can we move then, please, to the 9th of June. As I say, I'm missing out a number of entries on which you have commented, but that's all in your report. Which we'll find, it's the same P1755, and it's at page 121. The 9th of June meeting of the Presidency, and we see Karadzic, Koljevic, Plavsic, Krajisnik, Deric, Mladic, Gvero, Tolimir, and the minute taker. Meeting begins: I briefed the state and political leadership about the situation at the front. So we don't often see this, but is it -- when it says "I," that's him talking, is it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would appear so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then, please, over the page to -- well, actually two pages, 123. Combat reports are to be forwarded to the president of the Presidency in person, coded. Are we talking there about combat reports from the Main Staff or from the 1st Krajina Corps or from all the corps? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say from this reference. I am -- I have not looked at the Main Staff as a functioning organisation, and I don't know if they compiled their own combat reports based on the individual corps, or whether, to save time, they simply forwarded on combat reports from the various corps. So I can't comment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I would add that it clearly indicates that issues of a military nature are to be briefed in at the highest level.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah. And then under the -- near the bottom of that, provide the army of the Serbian Republic with instructions on how to proceed with POs. And this is -- I mean, this apparently appears to be Krajisnik speaking, from the previous page. So that's suggesting it was the civilians who would be providing the army with -- the political leadership, sorry, providing the army?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may not necessarily read it that way. I would maybe -- if it is Krajisnik saying that, or whoever is saying that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, sorry. Just stop for a moment, I'm sorry, Mr. Brown. My fault. Perhaps we could go back to the previous page, which is 122, so that we can see it's Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe what he's saying is to the army, You are to write regulations on the issue of prisoners of war, rather than the nuanced where you said it. There was a regulation subsequently passed, I believe, in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we look, then, please, at a meeting on the 10th of June, which is at page 127. This one's at the Villa Bosanska in Belgrade on the 10th of June, and it's a meeting with the representatives of the Serbian People from BiH. And if we go to 129, please, we see Karadzic begin to speak. Is that -- above there is Miodrag Perisic; is that General Perisic?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Karadzic begins speaking. And if we go over the page to 130, Karadzic appears to be discussing the situation and says: We have full control of many of our territories, we feel revealed -- sorry - revealed - we feel relieved now that we have formed our army and 40 per cent of the economy of BH and Sarajevo and the strategic goals. So does it look as though Karadzic at this meeting is restating the goals of the Serbian People in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would suspect so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, can we move, then, please, to the 21st of June, I think it is, yes. Yeah, can we look at page 18 -- well, first 185 so we see where we are. This appears to be a meeting he's holding with the East Bosnia Corps, does it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if we go over the page, just so we can see who's speaking, at 186, we see somebody called Racic, Miroslav. Do you know who he was?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Transformation of the TO into the RSK is slow. It is carried out through the MUP which cooperates with the corps intelligence officers and Lieutenant-Colonel Sajic, who is still the commander of the Krajina TO, and does not intend to be under Talic's command. Lieutenant-Colonel Sajic, I think we've seen in various documents, we're talking here about the Autonomous Region of Krajina and not the RSK; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would seem so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah. And then the next page. Nenad Stevandic, on 21st of June, political commissar of the SOS, says that Karadzic and Mladic are traitors to the Serbian People. We only think of Sarajevo and Herzegovina. He was an operative of the SDS, the chief of security, of the Krajina MUP, with Nedjeljko Kesic behind -- is behind him, and the SOS serves for settling scores with Serbs who are not sufficiently good. And does this link in with the later report that we looked at, again this morning, of General Tolimir -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, we are just wondering what the purpose of your examination is just now. These parts of the diaries are in evidence. It doesn't seem to us that the witness is contributing much other than confirming that this is what it says. So if you have nothing else to -- wish to add to this, then I think we should perhaps round up.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm perfectly content in the sense that he, in the extra report that I'm going to ask to go -- to be admitted, he explains which entries support the themes that he's developed through his report. He doesn't, however, identify -- I mean, it simply gives the dates. But the specific entries are not. So if Your Honours are happy that I don't go into the specific part of what is sometimes long entries with him, well, then, I won't do it, with one exception.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I don't think we need this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can I, however, just one last entry, Your Honours, if I may. And that's for May 1993, which is P1767, at page 151. It's 4 of the English. Yes. To put it in context, there's a meeting in Banja Luka on 27th of May, 1993, and Colonel Bogojevic is speaking. Can you just remind us who Colonel Bogojevic was.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe he was a security officer of the corps, 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And he's talking about Simo Drljaca arriving, being the former chief of the Prijedor SUP. And can we go to the next page, please. He talks about earlier they buried around 5.000 bodies. And I'm sure that the world knows about these released prisoners. Drljaca came to leave this with us, and they want to get rid of it by burning, grinding, or some other way. There are all kinds of bodies. They've involved Subotic in this. The team includes Drljaca. He was in charge, even while this was being done, at the meeting where General Subotic; Arsic; Drljaca; me, that's Colonel Bogojevic, presumably; and Mile Matovic from the Banja Luka secretary SUP. I ask for your position. My position, they killed them so they should get rid of them. An investigation must be launched in connection with this case and the information retained well to prevent it getting into the hands of unauthorised people. Who's saying that? They killed them so they should get rid of them. Do you know?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I can't be sure. It's either General Mladic himself, which I think is probably most likely, as he seems to asterisk his own phrases, or it's the position of the security officer, Bogojevic. But I can't say for sure. But if I had to put one, I believe it's probably General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, thank you very much, Mr. Brown. Then in light of the Trial Chamber's indication, that's all I'm going to ask you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: It's just time for the break and there is another couple of minutes, but before we transfer the floor to the Defence, I would like to ask you one question, Mr. Brown. And the question concerns the comment that you have added a couple of times during the testimony here, namely that the army apparently deplored the counter-productive treatment by the MUP and by paramilitaries against Muslim and Croat civilians in Bosnia in 1992. Do you remember that you have commented on this aspect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, there were a number of references to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes. My question to you is: How do you interpret these indications by the army? And more specifically: Do you consider this as an expression of frustration with the army, that they are unable to do anything about it, they are unable to get through to the political leadership and to have the political leadership take some action on it; or on the other hand, do you see it as an indication by the army that, well, this is deplorable but it's part of the war and in the end it may also serve some purpose so we are not going to do anything about it? Which of these two interpretations would you offer, or any -- if you have a third interpretation, of these indications from the army? It's important for the Chamber to understand fully how you as a military expert view and assess these indications by the army.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The references that I do see are often linked to -- or are often -- there are a number of comments that this type of activity is going to cause problems for the military in that it acts as a recruiting drive for others who may come subsequently to confront the VRS. I think the Prijedor is one, I think there are another maybe one or two other references. So one of the components that I think the army are unhappy with is not -- is not the obvious one that this is outrageous behaviour that shouldn't be tolerated in a state that we are building; they almost caveat it with the fact that this type of activity, the fallout, is going to be on us, because we are going to have to fight people who are -- who have been -- who have heard about these or who have been moved out the territory and it will act as a recruiting sergeant for them. That's one area. Some of the other comments, I believe, are that, say, for example, in relation to looting or burning, is that they're not necessarily solely discriminatory in terms of Muslims and Croats, that there are some Serbs or others who are -- who are being victimised too. So that is one area. And then I think, generally, I see a lot of this through the optics of command. The military wants to be able to conduct operations without the distraction of this type of activity coming. In a way - it maybe getting back to the issue I pointed out before - the lack of really clear sympathy about -- you know, here you have, if you like, an organisation, the VRS I'm talking about, many of the staff officers who were professional military officers, the lack of sympathy for what is clearly going on seems to me very, very stark. And so I don't see it as the military saying, well this problem is so out of control, we are simply not able to deal with it, even -- we have the utmost sympathy for the Muslims and Croats, but we can't do anything. I don't see that at all. I think there's quite an overwhelming feeling that they know they have these -- this territory to control, they have a direction that's been given to them, that territory has been marked out, the language in other documents make it clear that the non-Serb population are a threat and will continue to be so if they stay in the territory, and they're happy to follow that. And that -- that's how I view much of the documentation. This lack of sympathy, this lack of balance in the military documents, I think, is very stark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we've got a copy, if we can give it to Mr. Brown, as he's got -- of the transcript of the video on Operation Corridor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we take the break now, to resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: While the witness is on his way back, Ms. Korner had -- I don't know if "applied" is the correct word, but they had referred to the matter that is still live, about lifting the MFI status of the four items in the basket that's the notebooks, where there were these discrepancies between the versions that had been tendered or laid over. And the -- we assume that the Defence has seen the Prosecution's notice and report of the 10th of January of this year, and before we formalise what we will say about the status of these exhibits, in light of the notice, we think it would be useful if we -- if the Defence, if they care to, have any observations about these apparent discrepancies. And if we could hear from them first thing tomorrow morning, we would rule by tomorrow -- we will rule tomorrow on the final status of these four items.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. We will give our observations tomorrow morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You had a question, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, is Your Honour -- are Your Honours inviting the Defence to reopen their argument on discrepancies and admission?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I was hoping I wasn't. That is why I tried to choose my words carefully. There is -- there was -- the process of this matter is there was the application, the Defence responded, we ruled, and the -- we thought that it would have -- once the necessary comparisons were made, it would have been a fairly straightforward exercise, but it appears, especially in relation to two of the entries, there is a question that may be raised, and we just wanted to have the benefit of any observations that the Defence may wish to make. And I emphasise that inasmuch as what the Prosecution tendered on the 10th of January is merely a notice at the request of the Chamber, in other words, it isn't a motion on which we are requesting their response, but because of what is on the face of the notice itself, we just would find it useful if the Defence, if they wish, first thing tomorrow morning, indicated any observations that they have.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Your Honour, as I said, at the end of today I want to mention something that has a bearing on the notebooks, and I maybe come back to it at that stage. Your Honours, I had actually completed my examination-in-chief, but Mr. Brown had a look at the transcript of the corridor video over the break and I don't know whether Your Honour or Mr. Brown feels there's anything useful he can add to Your Honours -- Judge Harhoff's questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I very briefly looked at it, Your Honour, and there just seems to be a statement from Martic that his troops have been involved and that they've suffered some casualties, but it doesn't go into any great detail about their exact role and what they've been doing there. I would have to probably look, as well, any other military documents that may have a bearing on that, but not from that video extract.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Suggesting that some parts of the police somehow were involved in direct combat activity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he does make reference to the fact he's had casualties and that they're going to continue on and that they're not going to be distracted by -- from that. It would seem that they've been involved in combat activities, although obviously casualties can occur in a number of ways.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to start my cross-examination by asking about your qualifications. During the examination conducted by my learned friend Ms. Korner we saw that there were some matters that might necessitate our going into private session. If your reply should make that necessary, please indicate that to me. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, you have some academic titles from two areas, that is, modern history and criminology; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You acquired specific military knowledge during the course you attended at Sandhurst academy; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was one component. I was a commissioned officer and spent time at the military academy, but obviously my specific military knowledge is not just from that course but my service as a military officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When I said "military knowledge," I was referring to theoretical knowledge.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, part of the military academy does deal with various components of military knowledge, and I did other staff courses whilst I was a serving officer so -- which, again, has both a theoretical component and a practical component. And then obviously there was my experience in operational situations when I was serving as an officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, sir, the course at Sandhurst military academy has a duration of 44 weeks, I believe; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: That may be the case now, yes. I'm not sure exactly what it is today, but it was just under a year when I did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because in our country, as in some other countries, military academies have a four-year curriculum such as in the United States, for example, at West Point. But that seems not to be the case in the British army, or is it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: The specific officer training is not a four-year course. Most officers nowadays are graduates who will have done some kind of graduate course prior to that. Officers in the American army can also go in and join the service not solely through West Point, which is a long course. They can go in through other avenues. But in relation to the military -- British military, it's that length of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I understood your CV correctly, then you served in active duty in Northern Ireland; then in the Middle East, during Desert Storm; and finally in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I don't know if this is worth -- if you're going to expand on that, whether this might be appropriate for a private session. I'm not sure, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, to be on the safe side, I would like us to move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir -- I apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: After your tours of duty in Northern Ireland, the Middle East, and Bosnia-Herzegovina, you found employment at the OTP of this Tribunal and you held the position of a military analyst; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And during your employment with the OTP, you were actively involved in the investigations conducted by the Prosecutor's Office; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In that sense, you took part in interviews and statement-taking from a number of witnesses; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: From a number, yes, I did, sir, yes, as part of - I hasten to say - a joint team, usually with a lawyer and a senior investigator.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But in a number of cases it was you who directly posed questions to either witnesses or other type of interviewees; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir. And I believe probably in a small number of cases, I did, yes, under the assistance of a senior legal representative, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is a fact that you participated in interviewing and witness statement-taking from witnesses pertaining or relating to this particular case; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure what you mean by "this particular case." I was asked to assist in the interview of a number of individuals from the Krajina area, but whether it was related to this particular case, I'm -- as you phrase it, I'm not quite sure. I was asked to assist in that process.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go briefly into private session for the benefit of refreshing the memory of this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, the investigating team would ask you to deal and analyse certain matters that they thought was of interest for their work; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Invariably it didn't really work like that. It tended to be I was set a task, in this case, to look at a series of documents. A lot of the material that the military analysis team worked on was documentary. I was asked to look at what the material said in its very general terms, and I would get material translated, I would systematically collate material, and I would review it. And it tended to be more the passage of information down to the investigation teams or to the legal teams, as the case was. It may have been, on occasion, an investigator would come and say, "Can you tell me are there any documents in relation to this, this, or this?" But for the purposes of my report, for example, which actually ended up being a significant component of my work, that was done through myself or my manager -- the team leader of the analysis team.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let us please be concise in your answers so as not to waste time. Now, if an investigator or a counsel for the Prosecution is, for example, specifically interested, as we heard today, in the role of the RSK police in the Corridor Operation; in that case, they would approach you and ask you to furnish them with the document and to establish whether that is a fact and to provide corroborating documents confirming the fact; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: They could do, through the team leader. He would clearly need to know about the tasks that were being set his analysts. So there were regular management meetings at which if that was a specific task, an analytical task, please provide me an analysis of what you believe to be the involvement of the RSK MUP in operations. That might be set as a task to the team manager, and he would allocate that to an analyst for him to work on over a protracted period of time. There may also be a request to say, "That combat report which you flagged up to me, is there anything else that would -- that are similar to that around that period?" But it tended to be -- most of the tasks set to the military analysts were longish-term analysis, for example, my report and similar reports that were being written by other analysts. After all, the investigators normally were able to access material, documentary material, that we were too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's quite clear to me. However, it was them who suggested to you which specific matters you are required to analyse for their purposes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Although I would have to say there were also times, for example, when I started reviewing the material in the Krajina Corps, I believe the suggestion to write -- to write the report was -- was done generally through a management team when it became clear that this material was useful. But the investigators had the opportunity to come and speak to analysts and ask certain questions of them and, you know, know if they highlighted particular documents or materials.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let us focus only on this document that you produced on the 27th of November, 2002, and it is entitled, "The analysis of the situation." You prepared this analysis on the basis of the request for such an analysis to be carried out and conducted; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And after you had finished the analysis, you sent it to the party that had requested it - whether it was an investigation team or a team conducting certain cases, it doesn't matter - at any rate, that analysis was passed on to them?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. I mean, there was a process before it was disseminated out to others, a peer review process, internally, within the team, and it was reviewed by my manager. And then once that happened, it was disseminated to -- to the team that had -- was interested in it, and more widely, I have to say, within the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And surely, after this initial analysis has been discussed at length within the analytical team and it was thereafter sent to the requesting party, the requesting party would come back to you with some feedback in terms of additional requests or additional clarifications and things of that nature; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe there were some discussion after the report was produced. I'm not sure that there was too much of a request or too many requests, after I had completed it, to -- to clarify or add in anything. I don't really remember too much of that. But, yes, there were meetings after the report had been finished about whether -- you know, its content. I was not asked to change anything after that -- it was published, I hasten to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's perfectly clear. Once it's been published and distributed to the Defence teams, there was no reason whatsoever for any alterations to be made in the document because, as you said, during these meetings within the OTP, its content had been finalised; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I think that's true. I'd accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On page 18632 of the transcript, you confirmed that this report is based exclusively on the documents that is in the possession of the OTP. And the day before yesterday, you confirmed that this primarily refers to the documents popularly known as the 1st Krajina Corps document collection.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is predominantly from military documents of that corps. There are one or two -- there are a few, quite a few, documents which are not from that collection, but it's predominantly from that corps collection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you previously agreed with me that this document was first finalised within the OTP before its being published and disseminated to the Defence teams, you would agree with me, wouldn't you, that that has a considerable impact on the impartiality of this report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I would agree with you there, sir, at all. The report, when it was written initially, at least from my perspective, was not one that was destined for court use. It was a document that I'd been asked to look at these -- this collection and compile a report on what I believed to be some of the salient issues that came from it. How the Prosecution decided to use it was up to them. But I wouldn't agree with you that it necessarily has a -- or necessarily has an impact on its impartiality. There are limitations to the report, undoubtedly, and I'm very open to say that there are limitations. It is a document collection, for one, document-heavy report. It's predominantly from, as you said, from the documents of the 1st Krajina Corps. That has a limitation. It's limited in terms of its time. It looked at areas from round about late 1991 and end of 1992, predominantly. It has limitations in that I don't speak B/C/S, so I'm relying very heavily on the translations. So there are limitations to the report, and I'm happy to accept those. But I don't necessarily agree with you at all that the way that it was compiled or given to the Defence teams somehow impacts on its impartiality.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. We'll get back to this when we come to specific --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, in the first part of your answer, you said that the report was, as it was written initially, you didn't consider that it was destined for court use. You prepared it at the request of the Prosecution and it was up to them to make such use of it as they did. Had you anticipated that it would be quote/unquote, "for court use," would anything have changed, either in the way you -- either in the analysis itself or in the way that you presented the analysis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not at all, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My training in the military and the reports I've had to write there, to military commanders, reports I've written in the past, you know, I hope that they stand for what they are. Whether they were going to be used in court or not, this report, I believe, was one of the early reports that was really written in the team, large reports, that is. And I didn't necessarily think it was going to be used in court or not, and -- but that wouldn't have affected the way I had written it at all, sir. You know, I stand by what I wrote at the time and to the best of my ability compiled a report that I thought reflected what the corps documents said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said we would go back to this matter when we come to comment specific parts of your report. But it's a fact that the report has three parts, the political-military situation, military operations, and the role and the powers of the corps commanders; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I hope you will agree with me when I say that a familiarity with the military tradition and the military doctrine, as well as the rulings and regulations upon which the organisation structures of the armed forces, is something one must know in order to compile such a report and/or understand it.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: By that do you mean you have to have been in the VRS or the JNA to understand that? Is that your position? Is that the question? When you say "familiarity," does that mean you have to have been in that organisation? I'm a little bit unclear on the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I may not have been clear enough. I'll try to phrase it differently. If I, for example, should want to write an analysis about something in the British army, and supposing that I had the qualifications that I don't have, for me to be able to do that, I would certainly have to be familiar with the basic rules and regulations in force in the British military, such as the law on the armed forces, I believe it's called the NSS, namely the National Security Strategy, and some other documents; am I right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I guess it depends on what the purpose of your analysis is. If your analysis is to look on the law of the army, then, you know, if you're a researcher or a talented researcher there's no reason why you can't, you know, do work that would be -- that would be -- would stand up to peer review in that area. I guess it all relates to your skills as a researcher. And clearly, a familiarity, for example, my own experience in the military -- British military, would stand me in some stead if I had to write about certain aspects of the British military; that might be greater than someone who had not searched in the British military.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'll try for the third time. If I wanted to write an analysis of the military operations of the British army, such as carried out in a certain time period, I would have to be familiar with the Law on the Army, study it thoroughly, then the rules of service in the British army, its strategy, its tactics, and so on; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not necessarily. If your analysis of operations in a particular zone were limited, then your report would be limited. You don't have to know every single issue related to the British army. If it was to do with the Law on the Army, legal issues, then clearly you would have to know. I guess it depends on what the definition of your task is. It's a somewhat rather large -- an analysis of military operations of the British army; it's a rather large topic. Maybe what I'm saying is it depends on what you've been asked to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm proceeding by the sections into which you divide your analysis. Section 2 is entitled, "Military Operations of the 1st Krajina Corps in 1992." Section 3 is called, "Roles, Responsibilities, and Authorities of the Commander of the Corps." Are you trying to say that even for this third section it is not a must to know the rules of service as well as the other rules and regulations in force and pertaining to the roles, responsibilities, and authorities of corps commanders? Is that what you're trying to say to me?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm saying that that section of the report was in there as the documents in the corps collection reflected. Of course it was -- it is of value to know about the law of the army or doctrinal issues and it does help, but your question seemed to be somewhat general. I'm saying, if you have to conduct an analysis or research, what goes in depends on what the task that has been set is, it would seem to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's simplify things. In your opinion, to carry out the task that you were assigned within the OTP, namely the drafting of this analysis of the situation in 1992, which is divided into three sections, namely political military developments, military operations, and rules, responsibilities, and authorities, do you think that to carry out this task it is necessary for you to have analysed and familiarised yourself with the military tradition, rules and regulations in force in the JNA, rules in force for combat operations, strategy and tactics of the former JNA? Is that necessary to accomplish such a task or not?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I analysed the materials I was able to get from the 1st Krajina Corps on those topics. Are you asking me am I an expert in every issue relating to the JNA and its traditions, rules, and regulations, the answer would be, not necessarily, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this, Mr. Brown, because I noticed, in the entire document which is about 200 pages long, at least in the Serbian version, that very rarely, if at all, you refer to any rules of engagement or any regulations to explain an event or an activity carried out by the 1st Krajina Corps or its subordinate units. Do you agree with what I've put to you?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I do agree with you, actually. I think there are references explaining an event or activity by the 1st Krajina Corps. They themselves make a lot of references to that. And there are references in the report to doctrinal issues. I haven't seen, specifically, a document that discusses what I would know to be rules of engagement, which are a very specific military regulation, I guess. But there are documents in here that talk about wider regulations. There are documents that were in the collection that talked about doctrinal issues. For example, provisional Law on the Army and others. So I wouldn't agree with you, I think, in your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: While you were drafting this analysis of yours, did you rely on or read the corps rule of the JNA, which is a kind of combat rule?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read the regulations. I'd have to refresh my memory. I believe there was a 4th Corps regulation, a provisional regulation, from late 1991 which I believe I read. I think it's referenced, but I would have to look at it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you use in your analysis, or do you refer to, the rules of service in the JNA or the armed forces of the former SFRY?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I did. I'd have to check my references again, though, to be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: While drafting this analysis, did you use the law on All People's Defence and social self-protection of the former SFRY?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I referenced it. I maybe didn't footnote it, but I think I have referenced it. You're talking about the Law on All People's Defence, sir? I believe I referenced it in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: While you were drafting this report, did you use an additional document, the name of which I'm going to quote now: "The Strategy of All People's Defence and Social Self-Protection of the SFRY from 1987"?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think I believe that I used that document or reviewed it, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I remember that Ms. Korner was asking for two minutes before we break, and I think this is a proper place where I could break and continue tomorrow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we needn't trouble the witness. The witness can leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Brown, you are excused, to continue tomorrow morning. The usher will escort you from the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, the matter is this: In the Seselj Trial Chamber, publicly announced was the report that the Seselj Trial Chamber sought on handwriting in respect of the Mladic notebooks. Your Honours, the situation is this: Your Honours declined to let us call surrounding evidence as to the authenticity, for example, from the investigator who took the books and the like. And we're assuming that therefore, and indeed you've ruled, that you're satisfied the Mladic notebooks are authentic. But we feel it right, so that it's on the record, to say particularly in the light of your -- the invitation to the Defence to respond to Mr. Hannis's notice, that there is further evidence which we would be applying to call if there is any further challenge to the authenticity of the notebooks. That's just so it's plain for everybody to see. We haven't put it -- sought to put it in because we're reluctant to increase the number of outstanding matters at the moment, and, as I say, you have already ruled. But I think we ought to put it on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Ms. Korner. And let me say that we would be surprised if the observations which the Defence makes in -- at the invitation of the Chamber are in effect a challenge to the authenticity of the notebooks. It's merely, I would have thought, a question of what precisely it is that has been admitted, because the Chamber has, in fact, admitted the documents. It's merely a question of which is the ones that are going to be -- which of the actual ones that have been admitted, as opposed to the MFIs it would formulate. Thank you. So we take the adjournment to tomorrow morning.
